cse-2009-cs-41.approach: Read off what each state remembers about the suffix read so far: q0 = "does not end in 0", q1 = "ends in exactly one 0", q2 = "ends in 00". The accepting state is q2, so the language is strings ending with 00; then kill the other options with one-string counterexamples.

steps.title: Meaning of each state
steps.body:
Every **1** (from any state) goes to $q_0$, so $q_0$ means "the input is empty or ends in 1".

A **0** from $q_0$ goes to $q_1$: $q_1$ means "ends in exactly one 0".

A **0** from $q_1$ or $q_2$ goes to $q_2$: $q_2$ means "ends in at least two 0s", i.e. ends with $00$.

steps.title: Trace 0100
steps.body: $q_0 \xrightarrow{0} q_1 \xrightarrow{1} q_0 \xrightarrow{0} q_1 \xrightarrow{0} q_2$ — accepted, and $0100$ ends with $00$.

steps.title: Counterexamples for the other options
steps.body:
- $1$: $q_0 \to q_0$, rejected, yet it begins with 1 — so not (A).
- $0$: $q_0 \to q_1$, rejected, yet it ends with 0 — so not (B).
- $001$: $q_0 \to q_1 \to q_2 \to q_0$, rejected, yet it contains $00$ — so not (D).

The accepted language is exactly the strings ending with $00$.

animation.caption: Trace of 0100 from the start state q0

answer.value: The DFA accepts exactly the strings that end with 00 — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: Every string starts with 0 or 1, but e.g. $1$ is rejected (stays in $q_0$).
The string $0$ ends with 0 but stops in non-accepting $q_1$; one trailing 0 is not enough.
Only $q_2$ accepts and $q_2$ is reached exactly when the last two symbols are $00$.
$001$ contains $00$ but the final 1 sends it back to $q_0$, so it is rejected.

pitfalls: Reading the $q_2 \to q_0$ arc on 1 as "stay accepted" — any trailing 1 resets to $q_0$, so "contains 00" is wrong.
cse-2009-cs-41.verification: Checked $\varepsilon$, $0$, $00$, $100$, $001$, $0100$: accepted exactly when the string ends in $00$.

cse-2009-cs-42.approach: Judge each statement from compiler fundamentals: deterministic parsers (LL/LR) are linear; recursion needs a run-time stack; S-attributed definitions are L-attributed and are evaluated bottom-up; optimisation happens on source and IR.

steps.title: Statement I — true
steps.body: LL(1) and LR(1) parsers run in $O(n)$ time, which is less than $\Theta(n^3)$ (the bound for general CYK/Earley parsing). Most programming languages have such grammars.

steps.title: Statement II — false
steps.body: With recursion several activations of the same procedure are alive at once, each needing its own locals. Static allocation gives one fixed copy per procedure, so recursion needs stack (or heap) allocation.

steps.title: Statement III — false
steps.body: Every S-attributed definition is L-attributed and is evaluated directly during bottom-up (LR) parsing; even inherited L-attributes can be handled bottom-up with marker non-terminals. So "no L-attributed definition" is false.

steps.title: Statement IV — true
steps.body: Code-improving transformations (e.g. loop restructuring at source level, common-subexpression elimination on three-address code) are applied both at source and intermediate-code level. True statements: **I and IV**.

answer.value: Statements I and IV are true — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: II is false: recursion cannot be implemented with static storage allocation.
I (linear-time LL/LR parsers exist) and IV (optimisation at source and IR level) are both true.
III is false: S-attributed definitions are L-attributed and evaluate bottom-up.
Includes the false statement III.

pitfalls: Treating "L-attributed" as "has inherited attributes" — S-attributed definitions are a subset of L-attributed ones.
cse-2009-cs-42.verification: Each statement checked against a concrete case: LR(1) is linear, recursive factorial needs per-call frames, YACC evaluates S-attributed rules bottom-up.

cse-2009-cs-43.approach: Draw the precedence graph for each schedule: add $T_i \to T_j$ for every conflicting pair (same item, at least one write) where $T_i$'s operation comes first. A schedule is conflict-serializable iff the graph is acyclic.

steps.title: Conflicting pairs
steps.body: $T_2$ never writes $x$, so on $x$ the only conflict is $R_2[x]$ vs $W_1[x]$. On $y$ the conflicts are $R_2[y]$ vs $W_1[y]$ and $W_1[y]$ vs $W_2[y]$. ($R_1[x]$ conflicts with nothing in $T_2$.)

steps.title: S1 — cycle
steps.body: $R_2[x] < W_1[x]$ gives $T_2 \to T_1$; $W_1[y] < W_2[y]$ gives $T_1 \to T_2$. Cycle $T_1 \rightleftarrows T_2$ ⇒ **not** conflict-serializable.

steps.title: S2 — acyclic
steps.body: $R_2[x] < W_1[x]$, $R_2[y] < W_1[y]$ and $W_2[y] < W_1[y]$ all give $T_2 \to T_1$. Only one direction ⇒ serializable, equivalent to $T_2\,T_1$.

steps.title: S3 — acyclic
steps.body: $W_1[x] < R_2[x]$, $W_1[y] < R_2[y]$ and $W_1[y] < W_2[y]$ all give $T_1 \to T_2$ ⇒ serializable, equivalent to $T_1\,T_2$.

steps.title: S4 — cycle
steps.body: $R_2[x] < W_1[x]$ gives $T_2 \to T_1$; $W_1[y] < W_2[y]$ gives $T_1 \to T_2$ ⇒ cycle, **not** serializable. Serializable schedules: $S_2$ and $S_3$.

answer.value: $S_2$ and $S_3$ are conflict-serializable — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: $S_1$ has the cycle $T_2 \to T_1$ ($x$) and $T_1 \to T_2$ ($W_1[y]$ before $W_2[y]$).
$S_2$ has only $T_2 \to T_1$ edges and $S_3$ only $T_1 \to T_2$ edges — both acyclic.
$S_2$ is also conflict-serializable, so "$S_3$ only" is incomplete.
$S_4$ has a cycle, exactly like $S_1$.

pitfalls: Counting $R_1[x]$ vs $R_2[x]$ as a conflict — two reads never conflict.
cse-2009-cs-43.verification: Swapping non-conflicting operations turns $S_2$ into $R_2[x]R_2[y]W_2[y]R_1[x]W_1[x]W_1[y]$ = serial $T_2T_1$, and $S_3$ into serial $T_1T_2$.

cse-2009-cs-44.approach: Simulate the insertions. A leaf holds at most 2 keys, so a third key forces a split. Taking the split that keeps leaves full on the left (2 keys left, 1 right, separator = largest key of the left leaf, keys ≤ separator go left) maximises the splits and gives 4.

steps.title: Insert 10, 3, 6
steps.body: $[10] \to [3,10]$. Inserting 6 overflows: $[3,6,10] \Rightarrow [3,6]\,|\,[10]$, separator 6 goes up to a new root. **Leaf split 1.**

steps.title: Insert 8
steps.body: $8 > 6$ goes to the right leaf: $[10] \to [8,10]$. No split.

steps.title: Insert 4
steps.body: $4 \le 6$: $[3,4,6] \Rightarrow [3,4]\,|\,[6]$, separator 4 goes up; root $[4,6]$ has 3 pointers (allowed). **Leaf split 2.**

steps.title: Insert 2
steps.body: $2 \le 4$: $[2,3,4] \Rightarrow [2,3]\,|\,[4]$, separator 3 goes up. **Leaf split 3.** The root $[3,4,6]$ now needs 4 pointers > 3, so it splits: 4 moves up, giving $[3]$ and $[6]$ below root $[4]$.

scene.caption: Leaf splits so far: 3 (plus one internal split)

steps.title: Insert 1
steps.body: $1 \le 4$, $1 \le 3$: $[1,2,3] \Rightarrow [1,2]\,|\,[3]$, separator 2 joins $[3]$ to make $[2,3]$ (3 pointers, allowed). **Leaf split 4.** Total leaf splits $= 4$.

answer.value: With the left-full split the leaves split 4 times — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: 2 is below even the minimum count (3) obtained with right-heavy splits.
3 is what right-heavy splits ($[3]\,|\,[6,10]$, $[6]\,|\,[8,10]$, $[2]\,|\,[3,4]$) give; 4 and 1 then fit without splitting — not the maximum.
Left-full splits with "key ≤ separator goes left" give 4 leaf splits (the accepted answer).
5 needs the left-full split combined with separator = smallest key of the right leaf, which also sends 8 left; this convention is not the one the accepted key uses.

pitfalls: Counting the internal (root) split as a leaf split — the question asks only about leaves.
The count depends on the split/separator convention (3, 4 or 5 are all obtainable); the accepted key is 4.
cse-2009-cs-44.verification: Final tree: root $[4]$; $[2,3] \to [1,2],[3],[4]$; $[6] \to [6],[8,10]$ — all 7 keys present in sorted leaf order, every leaf ≤ 2 keys, every internal node ≤ 3 pointers.

cse-2009-cs-45.approach: Recognise relational division $r \div s$: tuples $t$ over $R-S=\{a,b\}$ that appear with **every** $c$ in $s$. Check which queries express "for all $u$ in $s$, $(t,u) \in r$".

steps.title: Query I is division
steps.body: $\pi_{R-S}(r) \times s$ = every candidate $(a,b)$ paired with every $c$. Subtracting $\pi_{R-S,S}(r)$ leaves the missing pairs; their $(a,b)$ parts are the disqualified tuples. $\pi_{R-S}(r)$ minus those $= r \div s$.

steps.title: Query II is division
steps.body: $\forall u \in s\; \exists v \in r\,(v[S]=u \wedge v[R-S]=t)$ says $(t,u) \in r$ for every $u \in s$ — exactly the definition of $r \div s$.

steps.title: Queries III and IV are not
steps.body: III quantifies over **all** $v \in r$ and requires $t = v[R-S]$ for each — it is non-empty only if $r$ has a single $(a,b)$ value and every $c$ of $r$ is in $s$. IV is $\pi_{a,b}(r \bowtie s)$: an $(a,b)$ qualifies if it matches **some** $c$ in $s$, not all. So I ≡ II.

answer.value: Queries I and II are equivalent (both compute $r \div s$) — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: I (algebraic division) and II (calculus with $\forall u \in s$) both compute $r \div s$.
III quantifies over every tuple of $r$, not over $s$; it is not division.
IV is a join + projection (exists one matching $c$), not "for all $c$".
III and IV compute different, non-division results.

pitfalls: Confusing "some matching $c$" (join) with "every $c$" (division).

cse-2009-cs-46.approach: Recall RSA: encryption and decryption are exponentiation modulo $n$, and the exponents are inverses modulo $\phi(n)$ so that $M^{ed} \equiv M \pmod n$ by Euler's theorem.

steps.title: Key relation
steps.body: Choose $e$ coprime to $\phi(n)=(p-1)(q-1)$ and $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$, i.e. $ed = 1 + k\phi(n)$. So III is correct and II ($\bmod\, n$) is not.

steps.title: Encryption/decryption
steps.body: $M' = M^e \bmod n$ and $(M')^d = M^{ed} = M \cdot (M^{\phi(n)})^k \equiv M \pmod n$. So I is correct; IV (working $\bmod\,\phi(n)$) does not recover $M$ since $M$ may exceed $\phi(n)$ and Euler's theorem is mod $n$.

answer.value: Equations I and III describe RSA — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: II is wrong: the exponents are inverses modulo $\phi(n)$, not modulo $n$.
I (exponentiation mod $n$) and III ($ed \equiv 1 \bmod \phi(n)$) are the RSA equations.
Both II and IV are wrong.
IV is wrong: messages are exponentiated modulo $n$, not $\phi(n)$.

pitfalls: The question swaps the usual names (private $(e,n)$, public $(d,n)$); the equations are symmetric so it does not matter.

cse-2009-cs-47.approach: Sequence numbers must never repeat while an older packet carrying the same number may still be alive. A packet can live 64 s, so the sequence numbers of a connection must move on by at least one every 64 s: minimum rate $= 1/64$ per second.

steps.title: What must be avoided
steps.body: The ISN comes from a ToD clock (1 tick/ms, low 32 bits), so it never restarts from a fixed value after a crash. The remaining danger is a connection whose own sequence numbers advance so slowly that a number is reused while a duplicate with the same number is still in the network.

steps.title: Bound from the lifetime
steps.body: A duplicate disappears at most $T = 64$ s after it was sent. If the sequence number advances by at least 1 every 64 s, no two live packets share a number. Minimum rate $= \dfrac{1}{64\ \text{s}} = 0.015625/\text{s}$.

steps.title: Closest choice
steps.body: $0.0156/\text{s}$ is closest to $0.015/\text{s}$ (next option $0.064$ is 4× larger).

answer.value: About $1/64 \approx 0.0156$ per second, closest to $0.015/\text{s}$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: 0.064 is the lifetime in thousands of ms (64 s), not a rate.
No reading of the data gives 0.135/s.
No reading of the data gives 0.327/s.

pitfalls: The 32-bit clock wraps only every $2^{32}$ ms $\approx 49.7$ days, far longer than 64 s, so the clock itself is not the constraint.

cse-2009-cs-48.approach: An error pattern $E(x)$ goes undetected only if $G(x)$ divides $E(x)$. If $(1+x) \mid G(x)$, then $G(1)=0$; an odd number of errors gives $E(1)=1 \ne 0$, so $G$ can never divide $E$.

steps.title: Undetected errors
steps.body: Received $= T(x)+E(x)$ with $G \mid T$. The error escapes iff $G(x) \mid E(x)$.

steps.title: Evaluate at x = 1
steps.body: If $G(x) = (1+x)H(x)$ then $G(1) = 0$ (mod 2). An odd number of flipped bits means $E(1) = 1$. If $G \mid E$ then $E(1) = G(1)Q(1) = 0$ — contradiction. So every odd-weight error is detected.

answer.value: $G(x)$ must have $1+x$ as a factor — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: More than two terms is the condition for catching single-bit errors; it does not guarantee odd errors are caught — $G = 1+x+x^2$ (three terms) divides the 3-bit error $E = 1+x+x^2$.
Not dividing $1+x^k$ is the condition for detecting **double**-bit errors.
$(1+x) \mid G$ forces $G(1)=0$, while odd-weight $E$ has $E(1)=1$.
An odd number of terms means $G(1)=1$, i.e. $1+x$ does **not** divide $G$ — the opposite of what is needed.

pitfalls: Mixing up the double-error condition (B) with the odd-error condition (C).
cse-2009-cs-48.verification: $G = 1+x$: $E = 1+x+x^2$ (3 errors) leaves remainder $1$ — detected. $G = 1+x+x^2$ (odd terms) divides $E = 1+x+x^2$ — missed.

cse-2009-cs-49.approach: Check each statement against the standard DFD rules (Rajib Mall's list of common DFD mistakes, from which these statements come): one bubble in the context diagram, external entities only in the context diagram, no control information, data stores connect only to processes.

steps.title: I and III — true
steps.body: The context (level-0) diagram shows the whole system as a **single bubble** with its external entities. A DFD shows data movement only; control information (e.g. "if error, go to …") must not appear.

steps.title: II — false
steps.body: External entities appear **only in the context diagram**. Lower-level DFDs refine bubbles and keep the data flows balanced with the parent, but do not redraw the external entities — showing them at all levels is a listed beginner mistake.

steps.title: IV — false
steps.body: A data store can be read or written only by a **process** (bubble). Store-to-store or store-to-entity flows are not allowed. True statements: **I and III**.

answer.value: Only statements I and III are true — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: II is false (entities only in the context diagram).
II and IV are false.
I (single bubble) and III (no control information) are the true rules.
Includes II, which is false: external entities are shown only in the context diagram.

pitfalls: Confusing "balancing" (flows of a child DFD must match the parent bubble) with redrawing external entities at every level.
cse-2009-cs-49.verification: Rajib Mall, *Fundamentals of Software Engineering*, "commonly made errors while constructing a DFD model" lists: more than one bubble in the context diagram, external entities at all levels, control information in DFDs, and data stores connected to anything but bubbles — matching I, III true and II, IV false.

cse-2009-cs-50.approach: Use $V(G) = E - N + 2$ and compare it with the cycle count of the control-flow graph itself. The CFG (without an extra exit→entry edge) has only $E - N + 1$ independent circuits, so I is false; II and III are standard facts.

steps.title: Statement I — false
steps.body: For a connected graph the number of linearly independent circuits (cyclomatic number) is $E - N + 1$, but $V(G) = E - N + 2$. Example: if–else diamond, $N=4$, $E=4$: $V(G)=2$, independent circuits $=1$. McCabe's equality needs the extra exit→entry edge, which the program's CFG does not have.

steps.title: Statement II — true
steps.body: For binary decisions $V(G) = \pi + 1$, where $\pi$ is the number of decision (predicate) nodes: the diamond has 1 decision, $V = 2$ ✓.

steps.title: Statement III — true
steps.body: $V(G)$ is the number of linearly independent paths in a basis set, i.e. the number of paths to test for basis-path coverage. True statements: **II and III**.

answer.value: Statements II and III are true — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: I is false for the control-flow graph itself ($E-N+1$ circuits vs $V(G)=E-N+2$).
II ($\pi+1$) and III (number of independent test paths) are true.
Includes the false statement I.
Includes the false statement I.

pitfalls: Quoting McCabe's theorem (equal to the independent circuits of the strongly connected graph) without noticing it needs the added exit→entry edge.
cse-2009-cs-50.verification: Single loop (while): $N=3$, $E=3$ → $V=2$, independent circuits $=1$; 1 decision + 1 = 2 ✓; two basis paths (skip loop, enter loop) ✓.

cse-2009-cs-51.approach: Sectors are numbered sector-first, then surface, then cylinder (like digits of a mixed-radix number), so sector number $= c \cdot 1260 + h \cdot 63 + s$.

steps.title: Sectors per cylinder
steps.body: One cylinder holds $20 \times 63 = 1260$ sectors (10 platters × 2 surfaces = 20 surfaces), one track holds 63.

answer.value: Sector number 505037 — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: 505035 is 2 too small (off-by-two slip in the addition).
505036 is 1 too small (treats sectors as 1-based).
505038 is 1 too large.

pitfalls: Using 10 surfaces instead of 20 — each platter has 2 recording surfaces.

cse-2009-cs-52.approach: Invert the mixed-radix numbering: divide by 1260 for the cylinder, then the remainder by 63 for the surface; the last remainder is the sector.

steps.title: Cylinder
steps.body: One cylinder holds $20 \times 63 = 1260$ sectors (10 platters × 2 surfaces = 20 surfaces), one track holds 63. $1039 < 1260$, so $c = 0$ and the remainder is 1039.

pitfalls: Counting from 1: the 0th sector is ⟨0,0,0⟩, so the 1039th sector has number 1039.

cse-2009-cs-53.approach: Standard LCS recurrence: if the last characters match, extend the LCS of both prefixes by 1; otherwise drop the last character of one sequence or the other and take the better result.

steps.title: Matching last characters
steps.body: If $X[i-1] = Y[j-1]$ the character is in some LCS, so $\text{expr1} = l(i-1, j-1) + 1$. Neither (A) $l(i-1,j)+1$ nor (B) $l(i,j-1)$ is this.

steps.title: Different last characters
steps.body: If $X[i-1] \ne Y[j-1]$ at least one of them is unused: $\text{expr2} = \max(l(i-1,j),\, l(i,j-1))$ — option (C).

answer.value: $\text{expr2} \equiv \max(l(i-1,j), l(i,j-1))$ — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: Must use $l(i-1,j-1)+1$; $l(i-1,j)+1$ can over-count (e.g. X="aa", Y="a" gives 2).
$l(i,j-1)$ ignores the match and under-counts (X="a", Y="a" gives 0).
Correct mismatch case: skip the last symbol of X or of Y.
$l(i,j)$ on the right side is circular; and $l(i-1,j-1)$ alone can miss the better choice.

cse-2009-cs-54.approach: $L[i,j]$ depends only on $L[i-1,j-1]$, $L[i-1,j]$ and $L[i,j-1]$ — the cell above, left and above-left. Any order that fills these first works, so both row-major and column-major order are valid.

steps.title: Dependencies
steps.body: From the recurrence, $L[i,j]$ needs $L[i-1,j-1]$, $L[i-1,j]$, $L[i,j-1]$: all have row $\le i$ and column $\le j$, with at least one strictly smaller.

steps.title: Row-major and column-major both work
steps.body: Row-major: row $i-1$ is complete and $L[i,j-1]$ was just computed. Column-major: column $j-1$ is complete and $L[i-1,j]$ was just computed. So (B) holds and (C) is false.

steps.title: Other statements
steps.body: Only row 0 and column 0 need initial 0s (A is false: the rest is computed). (D) is too strong: $L[0,5]$ need not precede $L[1,0]$ even though $0 < 1$.

answer.value: The table may be filled in row-major or column-major order — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: Only the boundary row/column must be 0; interior cells are overwritten by the recurrence.
Both orders compute up, left and diagonal neighbours before the cell.
Contradicts (B); both orders work.
"Either $p<r$ or $q<s$" is not required — e.g. $L[0,5]$ and $L[1,0]$ are independent.

cse-2009-cs-54.verification: Filling a 3×3 LCS table for "ab"/"ba" in row-major and in column-major order gives the same final value 1.

cse-2009-cs-55.approach: Evaluate the nested NOT IN from the inside out. Inner: non-blue part ids. Middle: suppliers of some part that is NOT non-blue, i.e. of some blue part. Outer: suppliers not in that set — those who supplied no blue part. None of the options states this exactly; the accepted (official) key is (A).

steps.body: $P_{nb}$ = pids with color ≠ 'blue' (non-blue parts).

steps.title: Middle query
steps.body: Catalog rows whose pid is NOT IN $P_{nb}$ are rows for **blue** parts. So the middle query returns sids of suppliers who supplied **at least one blue part**.

steps.title: Outer query

steps.title: Matching to the options

(A) and the query differ only for suppliers with both blue and non-blue parts or with none, which the paper's key ignores.

cse-2009-cs-56.approach: List the FDs: only those implied by the keys sid and (sname, city). Every non-trivial FD then has a superkey on the left, which is exactly BCNF.

steps.title: Suppliers
steps.body: Keys: $\text{sid}$ and $(\text{sname},\text{city})$. FDs: $\text{sid} \to$ all, $(\text{sname},\text{city}) \to$ all; nothing else is given. Each determinant is a superkey ⇒ BCNF.

cse-2009-cs-57.approach: Count the frames that can be in flight inside the link at once: propagation time ÷ transmission time. Each needs a distinct sequence number, so $l = \lceil \log_2(\text{count}) \rceil$.

steps.title: Transmission time
steps.body: $T_t = \dfrac{1000\ \text{bits}}{10^6\ \text{bps}} = 1\ \text{ms}$.

steps.title: Frames in the link
steps.body: The link holds $\dfrac{T_p}{T_t} = \dfrac{25\ \text{ms}}{1\ \text{ms}} = 25$ frames back to back.

answer.value: $l = 5$ — option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^5 = 32 \ge 25$, the smallest that works.

pitfalls: Using the round trip ($1 + 2a = 51$ frames → 6 bits): the question asks only for frames packed in the link, and 6 is not an option.
cse-2009-cs-57.verification: 25 frames × 1 ms = 25 ms = propagation time ✓; 5 bits → 32 ≥ 25 ✓.

cse-2009-cs-58.approach: Timeline: the sender sends $2^5 = 32$ frames in 32 ms. The earliest acknowledgement for frame 1 is piggybacked on a 1000-bit data frame the receiver starts as soon as frame 1 arrives.

steps.title: Sender busy time
steps.body: Window $= 2^l = 2^5 = 32$ frames at $1$ ms each ⇒ last bit leaves at $t = 32$ ms.

steps.title: Earliest ack
steps.body: Frame 1 fully arrives at $1 + 25 = 26$ ms. The ack rides on a reverse data frame: $1$ ms to transmit + $25$ ms to propagate ⇒ received at $26 + 1 + 25 = 52$ ms.

steps.title: Waiting time
steps.body: Sender idles from $t = 32$ ms until the ack at $t = 52$ ms: $52 - 32 = 20$ ms.

cse-2009-cs-60.approach: Delete-max twice: move the last element to the root, then sift it down by swapping with the larger child until heap order holds.

steps.title: Delete 25
steps.body: Remove 25, move last element 12 to the root: $\{12, 14, 16, 13, 10, 8\}$. Larger child of 12 is 16 → swap: $\{16, 14, 12, 13, 10, 8\}$; 12 now has child 8 only, stop.

steps.title: Delete 16 — move 8 up
steps.body: Remove 16, move last element 8 to the root: $\{8, 14, 12, 13, 10\}$. Larger child is 14 → swap: $\{14, 8, 12, 13, 10\}$.

steps.title: Finish sift-down
steps.body: 8's children are 13 and 10; larger is 13 → swap: $\{14, 13, 12, 8, 10\}$. 8 is a leaf now.
